blocks.body:
A random variable is described completely by saying how its probability is spread out: which values it takes and how likely each one is, or, for a quantity such as a waiting time that can be any real number, how likely each interval is. That description is its distribution. Two random variables can come from completely different experiments and still have the same distribution, and then every probability question about one has the same answer for the other.

A handful of distributions turn up again and again, because each comes from a simple mechanism: counting successes in independent trials (binomial), waiting for the first success (geometric), counting rare events (Poisson), waiting for a rare event in continuous time (exponential), and adding up many small effects (normal). This lesson introduces them, together with the tools needed for continuous random variables: distribution functions and densities. It assumes [[random-variables]], the exponential function ([[exp-log]]) and the definite integral ([[riemann-integral]]).

blocks.title: Distribution function
blocks.body:
The (cumulative) distribution function of a random variable $X$ is
$$F_X(x) = \Pr(X \le x), \qquad x \in \mathbb R.$$
It is non-decreasing and right-continuous, it tends to $0$ as $x \to -\infty$ and to $1$ as $x \to \infty$, and $\Pr(a < X \le b) = F_X(b) - F_X(a)$ for $a < b$.

Every random variable has a distribution function, and $F_X$ determines the distribution of $X$, so it is the universal way of describing one.

blocks.title: Discrete distributions
blocks.body:
A random variable is discrete if it takes only finitely or countably many values. Its distribution is then given by the probability mass function $p(k) = \Pr(X = k)$, and $F_X$ is a step function that jumps by $p(k)$ at each value $k$. The basic examples, with their means and variances, are these.

- Bernoulli$(p)$: $\Pr(X = 1) = p$ and $\Pr(X = 0) = 1 - p$. Mean $p$, variance $p(1 - p)$. One trial that succeeds with probability $p$.
- Binomial$(n, p)$: $\Pr(X = k) = \binom nk p^k (1-p)^{n-k}$ for $k = 0, \dots, n$. Mean $np$, variance $np(1 - p)$. The number of successes in $n$ independent Bernoulli$(p)$ trials: each particular pattern with $k$ successes has probability $p^k(1-p)^{n-k}$, and there are $\binom nk$ such patterns.
- Geometric$(p)$: $\Pr(X = k) = (1-p)^{k-1} p$ for $k = 1, 2, \dots$. Mean $\frac1p$, variance $\frac{1-p}{p^2}$. The number of trials up to and including the first success.
- Poisson$(\lambda)$, for $\lambda > 0$: $\Pr(X = k) = e^{-\lambda} \frac{\lambda^k}{k!}$ for $k = 0, 1, 2, \dots$. Mean $\lambda$, variance $\lambda$. The number of occurrences of a rare event: misprints on a page, calls to a help line in a minute, decays in a radioactive sample in a second.

The binomial mean and variance come for free from [[random-variables]]: $X$ is a sum of $n$ independent indicators, each with mean $p$ and variance $p - p^2$. For the Poisson distribution, the probabilities sum to $1$ because $\sum_{k \ge 0} \lambda^k/k! = e^\lambda$, the exponential series ([[power-series]]), and the same series gives the mean:
$$\mathbb E[X] = \sum_{k \ge 1} k\, e^{-\lambda} \frac{\lambda^k}{k!} = \lambda e^{-\lambda} \sum_{k \ge 1} \frac{\lambda^{k-1}}{(k-1)!} = \lambda.$$
The same trick applied to $\mathbb E[X(X-1)]$ gives $\lambda^2$, so $\operatorname{Var}(X) = \mathbb E[X(X-1)] + \mathbb E[X] - (\mathbb E X)^2 = \lambda^2 + \lambda - \lambda^2 = \lambda$.

blocks.title: Poisson limit of the binomial
blocks.body:
Fix $\lambda > 0$ and an integer $k \ge 0$, and let $p_n = \lambda/n$. Then
$$\lim_{n \to \infty} \binom nk p_n^k (1 - p_n)^{n-k} = e^{-\lambda} \frac{\lambda^k}{k!}.$$

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
For $n > \max(k, \lambda)$ write
$$\binom nk \Big(\frac\lambda n\Big)^k \Big(1 - \frac\lambda n\Big)^{n-k} = \frac{\lambda^k}{k!} \cdot \frac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)}{n^k} \cdot \Big(1 - \frac\lambda n\Big)^n \cdot \Big(1 - \frac \lambda n\Big)^{-k}.$$
The second factor is the product of the $k$ numbers $\frac{n-j}{n} = 1 - \frac jn$ for $0 \le j < k$, each tending to $1$, and the fourth factor tends to $1$ because $k$ is fixed. The third tends to $e^{-\lambda}$ by the standard limit $(1 + x/n)^n \to e^x$ with $x = -\lambda$. Multiplying the limits proves the claim.

blocks.title: Rare events
blocks.body:
The theorem says that if there are many independent opportunities for an event, each with a small probability, the total count is approximately Poisson with mean $\lambda = np$, whatever $n$ and $p$ are individually. Here are the binomial probabilities for $n = 100$ and $p = 0.03$ next to Poisson$(3)$, rounded to four places:
$$\begin{array}{c|cccccc} k & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 \\ \hline \text{Binomial}(100, 0.03) & 0.0476 & 0.1471 & 0.2252 & 0.2275 & 0.1706 & 0.1013 \\ \text{Poisson}(3) & 0.0498 & 0.1494 & 0.2240 & 0.2240 & 0.1680 & 0.1008 \end{array}$$
This is why the Poisson distribution fits counts of misprints, accidents or decays so well: you never need to know the number of opportunities, only the average count.

blocks.title: Density
blocks.body:
A random variable $X$ is continuous with density $f$ if $f : \mathbb R \to [0, \infty)$ is integrable (possibly as an improper integral) with $\int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x)\,dx = 1$ and
$$\Pr(a \le X \le b) = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx \quad \text{for all } a \le b.$$
Then $F_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^x f(t)\,dt$, so $F_X' = f$ wherever $f$ is continuous (by the [[ftc|fundamental theorem of calculus]]), and the expectation is
$$\mathbb E[X] = \int_{-\infty}^\infty x f(x)\,dx, \quad \text{provided} \quad \int_{-\infty}^\infty |x| f(x)\,dx < \infty.$$

A density is not a probability but a probability per unit length: for small $h > 0$ and $f$ continuous at $x$, $\Pr(x \le X \le x + h) \approx f(x)\, h$.

blocks.title: Continuous distributions
blocks.body:
In the continuous case sums become integrals throughout; in particular $\mathbb E[g(X)] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(x) f(x)\,dx$, and the integrals over infinite intervals are [[improper-integrals]]. Three families do most of the work.

- Uniform$[a, b]$: $f(x) = \frac{1}{b - a}$ on $[a, b]$ and $0$ elsewhere. Mean $\frac{a+b}{2}$, variance $\frac{(b-a)^2}{12}$. A point chosen at random from an interval.
- Exponential$(\lambda)$, with rate $\lambda > 0$: $f(x) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x}$ for $x \ge 0$ and $0$ for $x < 0$, so that $\Pr(X > x) = e^{-\lambda x}$ for $x \ge 0$. Mean $\frac1\lambda$, variance $\frac1{\lambda^2}$. The waiting time for an event that happens at rate $\lambda$ per unit time, such as a radioactive decay.
- Normal $N(\mu, \sigma^2)$: $f(x) = \frac{1}{\sigma \sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-(x - \mu)^2/(2\sigma^2)}$ for all real $x$. Mean $\mu$, variance $\sigma^2$. The bell curve, which describes quantities made up of many small independent effects.

The exponential mean is an integration by parts ([[integration-techniques]]):
$$\int_0^\infty x\, \lambda e^{-\lambda x}\,dx = \Big[-x e^{-\lambda x}\Big]_0^\infty + \int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda x}\,dx = 0 + \frac1\lambda.$$

For the normal density, the fact that the total integral is $1$ amounts to $\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2/2}\,dx = \sqrt{2\pi}$, which is proved by squaring the integral and switching to polar coordinates ([[multiple-integrals]]). If $X$ is $N(\mu, \sigma^2)$, then $Z = (X - \mu)/\sigma$ is $N(0, 1)$, the standard normal distribution, whose distribution function is written $\Phi$. It has no elementary formula, but three values are worth memorising:
$$\Pr(|Z| \le 1) \approx 0.683, \qquad \Pr(|Z| \le 2) \approx 0.954, \qquad \Pr(|Z| \le 3) \approx 0.997.$$

blocks.title: Memorylessness
blocks.body:
If $X$ is exponential with rate $\lambda$, then for all $s, t \ge 0$,
$$\Pr(X > s + t \mid X > s) = \Pr(X > t).$$
Likewise, if $X$ is geometric with parameter $p$, then $\Pr(X > m + n \mid X > m) = \Pr(X > n)$ for all integers $m, n \ge 0$.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
For $x \ge 0$, $\Pr(X > x) = \int_x^\infty \lambda e^{-\lambda u}\,du = e^{-\lambda x}$. The event $\{X > s + t\}$ is contained in $\{X > s\}$, so
$$\Pr(X > s + t \mid X > s) = \frac{\Pr(X > s + t)}{\Pr(X > s)} = \frac{e^{-\lambda(s + t)}}{e^{-\lambda s}} = e^{-\lambda t} = \Pr(X > t).$$
For the geometric distribution, $\Pr(X > n) = (1 - p)^n$, since $X > n$ means that the first $n$ trials fail, and the same computation applies.

blocks.title: Transforming random variables
blocks.body:
If $X$ has a known distribution and $Y = g(X)$, the safest way to find the distribution of $Y$ is through distribution functions: compute $F_Y(y) = \Pr(g(X) \le y)$ by rewriting the event in terms of $X$, then differentiate to get the density.

For example, let $U$ be uniform on $[0, 1]$, fix $\lambda > 0$, and put $Y = -\frac1\lambda \ln U$ (the event $U = 0$ has probability $0$ and can be ignored). Since $\ln$ is increasing, for $y \ge 0$
$$\Pr(Y > y) = \Pr(\ln U < -\lambda y) = \Pr(U < e^{-\lambda y}) = e^{-\lambda y},$$
so $Y$ is exponential with rate $\lambda$. This is how a computer turns uniform random numbers into exponential ones. In general, if $F$ is continuous and strictly increasing, then $F^{-1}(U)$ has distribution function $F$, because $\Pr(F^{-1}(U) \le y) = \Pr(U \le F(y)) = F(y)$; this is called inverse transform sampling.

Not every random variable is discrete or continuous. Suppose you arrive at a traffic light at a random time, and the light is red half of the time, in phases of $60$ seconds. Your wait is $0$ with probability $\frac12$, and otherwise uniform on $(0, 60]$. Its distribution function jumps by $\frac12$ at $0$ and rises linearly to $1$ at $60$; there is no density and no mass function, but $F_X$ describes it perfectly well.

blocks.title: At least two sixes
blocks.body: A fair die is rolled $10$ times. Find the probability of at least two sixes, and the mean and variance of the number of sixes.
blocks.solution:
The number of sixes $X$ is Binomial$(10, \frac16)$. It is easiest to subtract the complementary cases:
$$\Pr(X \ge 2) = 1 - \Pr(X = 0) - \Pr(X = 1) = 1 - \Big(\frac56\Big)^{10} - 10 \cdot \frac16 \Big(\frac56\Big)^9.$$
Numerically this is $1 - 0.1615 - 0.3230 \approx 0.5155$. The mean is $np = \frac{10}{6} = \frac53$ and the variance is $np(1-p) = 10 \cdot \frac16 \cdot \frac56 = \frac{25}{18}$.

The Poisson approximation with $\lambda = \frac53$ would give $1 - e^{-5/3}\big(1 + \frac53\big) \approx 0.4963$. Here $p = \frac16$ is not small, and the approximation is only rough.

blocks.title: A lightbulb that does not age
blocks.body: The lifetime of a bulb, in hours, is exponential with mean $1000$. Find the probability that it lasts more than $1500$ hours given that it has already lasted $500$, and find the median lifetime.
blocks.solution:
Mean $1000$ means rate $\lambda = \frac{1}{1000}$. By memorylessness,
$$\Pr(X > 1500 \mid X > 500) = \Pr(X > 1000) = e^{-1} \approx 0.368,$$
exactly the probability that a new bulb lasts $1000$ hours. An exponential lifetime does not age: a bulb that has survived $500$ hours is as good as new. (Conversely, one can show that the exponential distributions are the only continuous distributions on $(0, \infty)$ with this property, which is why they model waiting times for events with no memory.)

The median $m$ solves $\Pr(X > m) = \frac12$, that is $e^{-m/1000} = \frac12$, so $m = 1000 \ln 2 \approx 693$ hours. Most bulbs fail before the mean lifetime, since $\Pr(X < 1000) = 1 - e^{-1} \approx 0.632$: a few very long-lived bulbs pull the mean up.

blocks.title: The square of a standard normal
blocks.body: Let $Z$ be standard normal. Find the density of $Y = Z^2$, and its mean.
blocks.solution:
Write $\varphi(z) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-z^2/2}$ for the standard normal density, so $\Phi' = \varphi$. For $y \le 0$ we have $F_Y(y) = 0$, since $\Pr(Z^2 \le 0) = \Pr(Z = 0) = 0$. For $y > 0$,
$$F_Y(y) = \Pr(-\sqrt y \le Z \le \sqrt y) = \Phi(\sqrt y) - \Phi(-\sqrt y).$$
Differentiating with the chain rule,
$$f_Y(y) = \varphi(\sqrt y) \cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt y} + \varphi(-\sqrt y) \cdot \frac{1}{2 \sqrt y} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi y}}\, e^{-y/2}, \qquad y > 0,$$
and $f_Y(y) = 0$ for $y \le 0$. The density is unbounded near $0$, but its integral is still $1$. The mean needs no new integral: $\mathbb E[Y] = \mathbb E[Z^2] = \operatorname{Var}(Z) + (\mathbb E Z)^2 = 1$.

This is the chi-squared distribution with one degree of freedom, which appears in statistics whenever squared errors are added up.

blocks.title: Breaking a stick
blocks.body: A stick of length $1$ is broken at two points chosen independently and uniformly at random. What is the probability that the three pieces form a triangle?
blocks.solution:
Let the break points be $X$ and $Y$. Because they are independent and uniform on $[0, 1]$, the pair $(X, Y)$ is uniformly distributed on the unit square: the probability that it lands in a region is the area of the region. (Formally, the pair has joint density $1$ on the square; densities of independent variables multiply.)

Three positive lengths with sum $1$ form a triangle exactly when each is less than $\frac12$, because the triangle inequality $a < b + c$ says $a < 1 - a$. Suppose first that $X < Y$. The pieces are $X$, $Y - X$ and $1 - Y$, and we need
$$X < \tfrac12, \qquad Y - X < \tfrac12, \qquad Y > \tfrac12.$$
These inequalities cut out the triangle with vertices $(0, \frac12)$, $(\frac12, \frac12)$ and $(\frac12, 1)$, of area $\frac18$. The case $Y < X$ is symmetric and gives another $\frac18$, and $X = Y$ has probability $0$. So the answer is $\frac14$.

blocks.body:
- A density value is not a probability and can exceed $1$: the uniform density on $[0, \frac12]$ equals $2$ there. Only integrals of $f$ are probabilities.
- For a continuous random variable, $\Pr(X = x) = 0$ for every $x$, so $\Pr(X \le x) = \Pr(X < x)$. Probability zero does not mean impossible: $X$ does take some value.
- Conventions differ. The geometric distribution sometimes counts the failures before the first success (mean $\frac{1-p}{p}$) instead of the trials (mean $\frac1p$); the exponential distribution is sometimes parametrised by its mean $\frac1\lambda$ instead of its rate; and in $N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ the second parameter is the variance, not the standard deviation. Check which convention a source uses.
- The Poisson approximation to Binomial$(n, p)$ needs $p$ small; for $n = 10$ and $p = \frac16$ it is off by about $0.02$.
- When transforming, work with $F_Y$ first. Substituting $x = g^{-1}(y)$ into the density forgets the factor $|dx/dy|$ and, for a function such as $x^2$ that is not one-to-one, the second branch.

Sums of independent random variables are where the normal distribution earns its place: the central limit theorem in [[limit-theorems]] says that the standardised sum of many independent copies of any distribution with finite positive variance is approximately $N(0, 1)$. In a continuous-time Markov chain the time spent in a state before jumping is exponential, because the Markov property forces it to be memoryless ([[markov-chains]]).

The integral $\int_0^\infty x^{s-1}e^{-x}\,dx$ behind the moments of the exponential distribution is the [[gamma|gamma function]]. The probability generating function $\mathbb E[z^X]$, for example $(1 - p + pz)^n$ for the binomial, links distributions with [[generating-functions]], and Fourier transforms of densities (characteristic functions, see [[fourier-poisson]]) are the main tool for proving limit theorems. In measure-theoretic probability ([[lebesgue]]) a distribution is a probability measure on $\mathbb R$, and the Radon–Nikodym theorem says it has a density exactly when it gives probability $0$ to every set of length $0$. In number theory, Gallagher showed that a uniform version of the Hardy–Littlewood prime tuples conjecture implies that, for $n \le x$ chosen at random, the number of primes in $(n, n + \lambda \ln x]$ tends in distribution to Poisson$(\lambda)$ as $x \to \infty$. The result is conditional: the conjecture is still unproved. See [[probabilistic-nt]].

1. Show that the uniform distribution on $[a, b]$ has variance $\frac{(b-a)^2}{12}$.
2. Let $X$ and $Y$ be independent and exponential with rates $\lambda$ and $\mu$. Show that $\min(X, Y)$ is exponential with rate $\lambda + \mu$. (Compute $\Pr(\min(X, Y) > t)$.)
3. Let $X$ and $Y$ be independent Poisson variables with means $\lambda$ and $\mu$. Show that $X + Y$ is Poisson with mean $\lambda + \mu$.
4. Let $U$ be uniform on $[0, 1]$. Find the density of $U^2$ and check that it integrates to $1$.
